technique: time — how the poem moves through it, or holds still
lesson: Today we work on one technique. It is how a poem handles time. This poem holds time still for most of its length, then moves it forward near the end. Look at how it starts: "The barn door hangs on its hinge half-wide." That door is stopped partway. Then "the hills sit patient." Nothing is moving yet. The poem keeps you in a held moment, like a photograph. Then time starts up again: "Now the pale is firming into something like light." The word "Now" tells you time is moving. Day is coming. The thing on the bench has waited long enough. Holding time still first makes the change feel like a push to act. You waited; now you go. Try this: describe one scene where nothing moves for several lines, then use the word "now" to start time again. The second time through, listen for where the stillness breaks. Here is the poem.
poem:
The barn door hangs on its hinge half-wide,
neither shut against the cold nor swung to the day,
the way a thing waits when you've left it mid-thought.
Out past the frost-stiff grass the hills sit patient,
holding the gray between one weather and the next.
You have been fussing a small thing to its finish—
a line gone clean, a dark speck made a dot,
turning it under the lamp till the edge rings true.
There's a satisfaction the hands keep to themselves,
the kind that comes of doing the fine part right.
Now the pale is firming into something like light,
and the half-made thing on the bench has waited long enough.

The thing you've been shaping is close now—
go put your own hands on it.
